facts.text: The AlCrCoFeNi alloy was heated in situ from room temperature to 1100 °C while high-temperature XRD tracked phase and oxide evolution.
The heating experiment compared low-oxygen vacuum exposure with exposure to atmospheric air.
Heating was performed at 10 °C/min in 50 °C increments, with a 5 min hold at each setpoint.
The vacuum experiment used an overall pressure of approximately 4.2×10^-6 atm; oxygen partial pressure was estimated as 8.82×10^-7 atm rather than measured directly.
Heating produced FCC at about 550–600 °C and Cr–Fe-rich sigma phase at about 600–650 °C, with sigma disappearing by roughly 950–1050 °C.
Oxidation proceeded mainly through outward diffusion and selective oxidation of Al, with Cr providing a secondary contribution.
Air exposure formed an Al2O3-rich outer scale over a thinner Cr2O3-rich inner region.
Greater Al consumption in air created an Al-depleted, B2-denuded subsurface transformation zone, whereas low oxygen availability limited this transformation.
Relative to vacuum exposure, atmospheric-air exposure produced substantially thicker oxidation and stronger subsurface phase transformation.
The duplex oxide scale formed in air was about 1.25 µm thick.
The outer alumina layer formed in air was approximately 1.08 µm thick.
Vacuum exposure produced a comparatively uniform, predominantly alumina oxide scale less than 0.5 µm thick.
